Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I can no longer trust my own body

vignette: When twelve‑year‑old Aisha first heard the scream that shattered her village, the sound was as bright as a flash of light and as sharp as the sting of a knife. She was running from a makeshift wooden structure that had collapsed around her, the air filled with the acrid taste of burning oil and the metallic tang of blood. The torture that followed—grappling, choking, the sensation of her throat constricting—left her body in a state of paralysis that seemed more a dream than a memory. In the weeks that followed, any time she was near another person’s house, the sudden clatter of a door, the distant hum of a passing truck, or the gentle rain that matched the night of her abduction would pull her back to that moment as if a trigger had opened a doorway to her past. These triggers, always felt before she could even process them, set her into a mode where she could not trust her own body, and they made the world feel like a hostile place. Because the triggers were always present, Aisha turned to concrete rituals to protect herself. Each morning she applied a heavy layer of makeup over the pale, scarred skin of her face, hoping the thick film would disguise her bruises and, more importantly, her fear. When a voice called her name from the hallway, she would immediately start a mental playlist of work songs, counting the rhythm so she could keep her mind occupied. She avoided clothing that resembled the rough fabrics she had been forced to wear in captivity, opting instead for soft, bright colors that she believed would shield her from the past. The sheer act of preparing herself for the day became a way of managing the sudden startle that would erupt at ordinary sounds: a door slam, a cough, a distant siren. Each time these triggers appeared, they escalated her sense of threat, reinforcing the belief that the world remained dangerous, that she was no longer capable of doing the work she once did, and that her body could no longer be trusted. Those negative appraisals, in turn, fed back into her coping rituals. Aisha began to believe that if she could not control her environment with heavy makeup and mental distractions, she would be powerless and that she would never recover her sense of self. The feeling that she was no longer capable of working as the diligent factory worker she had been before the torture, that the world was still a perilous place, and that her body betrayed her, led her to stay away from close contact with coworkers, to avoid eye contact, and to linger in the shadows of the breakroom instead of joining the lunchtime circle. The weight of these thoughts made her think that every decision to wear a certain shirt or to sit at a particular table was a risk to her safety, further entrenching her avoidance. At night, the memories of the torture surfaced with alarming fidelity. Aisha’s mind would replay the scene as if it were a film: a dark, cramped room, the rough grip of an assailant, the taste of blood. The story felt unreal, as if it belonged to someone else, yet the odor of burning oil would seep into her dreams, making the past feel present. When she recalled those moments, her body would react—her heart would race, her palms would sweat—before her mind could catch up. These memories, vivid and alien, made her feel as though she were being watched even when she was alone. The sensory cues from the past prompted her to keep her senses sharp, to listen for the slightest sound that might signal someone’s entry into her home. The memory of that night, with its disorienting quality and smell, had become a trigger in itself, pulling her back to the place where her body had first failed her. Because of this relentless cycle, Aisha’s threat monitoring grew so intense that even the faintest noise would cause her to jump. She would lock her doors, double‑check the windows, and, whenever possible, stay close to her workplace’s security office, where the constant hum of machinery provided a sort of buffer against the intrusive sounds that haunted her. She began to wear the same heavy makeup at work, as if it could ward off the phantom presence of her captor. Each time she saw her own reflection in a polished surface, the memory would flood back, and she would find herself applying more makeup to hide the shock of seeing the scarred skin and the way her eyes darted. The act of heavy makeup, in turn, reinforced her memory, because each brushstroke was a reminder of the night she could not trust her body. It is this interlocking web of triggers, negative beliefs, threats, memories, and coping strategies that has left Aisha’s life fragmented. Her work performance has dipped as she spends more time preparing herself than engaging in tasks, and she has withdrawn from social interactions with colleagues, fearing that any accidental proximity could awaken her terror. When she finally sought therapy, she explained that the constant state of hyper‑alertness was exhausting, that she was afraid her fear would consume every aspect of her life, and that she hoped, with professional help, she might reclaim her sense of agency and feel safe again.
